It is reflected in the deep, clear waters of our culture. Psychologists in the archipelago and the diaspora exhort the United Nations to fully implement Resolution 1514/15 as the sole route and necessary socio-psychological intervention to alleviate psychological trauma and promote the full health and well-being of Puerto Rico. I am a psychologist. Psychologists study conditions of well-being. Dr. Carol Reif's seminal research on psychological well-being established 6 distinct components of positive psychological health: 1, self-acceptance. According to Dr. Reeves, self-acceptance is expressed in having a positive attitude about oneself. We break the scale on that. Puerto Ricans love Puerto Rico, and I don't mean the shallow beaches. We are Puerto Rican culture. We are Bad Bunnies wherever we are. Two, personal growth is expressed in seeing oneself as growing and expanding, as open to explore one's greater potential. History evidences our readiness. The last 200 years of colonialism in Puerto Rico is the history of democratic and revolutionary struggles to establish an independent state that can anchor and lead the people to grow, expand, and explore our full potentials. 3, environmental mastery is expressing having the ability to have competence to manage one's affairs. There is no question the Puerto Ricans have the competence, skills, and education needed. What we do not have is the ability at this time to plan and employ Puerto Rican hands for Puerto Rican purposes. U.S. Congress Financial Control Board dictates all aspects of financial and governmental affairs. Four, autonomy is expressed in being self-determining and independent, able to resist social pressures on how to think and act. Yes, we are here to claim our autonomy, our independence and sovereignty as necessary for Puerto Rican psychological well-being. Five, purpose of life is expressing having direction and purpose that gives life a meaning. Puerto Rico's inalienable purpose as a people is to escape the poverty of colonialism and migrate to the safe harbor of independence where our children can freely develop their potentials and live in peace. 6, positive relations with others expressed in warm, satisfying, trusting relationships. My name is Jeremia Sedeño, co-founder of the Boric Collective, an organization dedicated to working for the well-being and survival of Puerto Rico, the world's oldest colony. Within a few weeks, the United States will be celebrating the 250th anniversary of their independence from Britain. Their very own Declaration of Independence says that "Whenever any form of government becomes destructive of these ends, it is the right of the people to alter or to abolish it and to institute new government." The abolishment of a destructive government was justified in their own Declaration of Independence, and yet they are entering year 128 of its destructive colonial rule over Puerto Rico. On June 30th, the Fiscal Oversight Board turns 10. In the decade since this board was introduced by Obama's Ley Promesa, all la Junta has done is aggressively carry out the colonial agenda of a Puerto Rico without Puerto Ricans. Total sovereignty over our finances are given to the unelected and presidentially appointed members of this junta. La Junta has closed over 600 schools, leading to a massive drain of talent from the archipelago. They've served in the best interest of Wall Street, allowing profit to be made off of our debt. LUMA gets to charge insane rates for an energy system that's always failing, and HMS makes millions off of Puerto Rico while providing poor service to vieques and culebra, an issue which recently cost the life of Sheila Sanabria. While the board imposed severe cuts to local public services, pensions, and social programs to repay bondholders, these lucrative tax exemptions have fueled gentrification and paved the way for projects like Essencia to try and destroy our coasts. Despite all these hardships, Puerto Ricans have shown a strong sense of national pride and self-respect. This was seen on full display when Speaker Number 51, the disgraced ex-governor of Puerto Rico, was ousted from his office. In closing, I hope that after 40 resolutions, decolonization, and independence, for the nation of Puerto Rico can become a reality. ¡Que viva Puerto Rico libre!

The University of Puerto Rico has eliminated more than 60 bachelor's degree programs, forcing many of our youth to leave their homeland in search for educational opportunities elsewhere. If Puerto Rico were presenting a constitution to the United Nations for the first time today, and that constitution contained an exception for legalized slavery, would this body approve and call it self-determination? I ask because the answer tells you everything about what has happened to Puerto Rico for the past 74 years. I'm Dennis Feeble, National Lead Organizer of the Abolish Slavery National Network. Puerto Rico abolished slavery under Spain in 1873. Absolutely no slavery exception. That is where Puerto Rico stood before 1898. Then the United States arrived and their federal 13th Amendment slavery exception came with the military occupation, an amendment Puerto Ricans did not ratify. And then came the Jones Act, carrying the same exception forward in 1917, which Puerto Rico did not vote for. And when Puerto Rico convened for their own constitutional convention in 1951, the delegates were offered the broader language: slavery and involuntary servitude, except as punishment. They rejected it. They confined the exception to involuntary labor alone, and they kept the prohibition on slavery absolute. They defined slavery on the floor as a subjection of a person to the will and power of another without recourse. That is slavery as status. They knew exactly what they were protecting. The enrolled text, the official engrossed version, reversed them anyway. It put the broader language back in. Both slavery and involuntary servitude became permissible as punishment. No floor debate, no second vote. The governing Spanish text now preserves the slavery exception the delegates voted down. What I have just described has a name in international law: jus cogens. No people can consent to slavery. No legislature can authorize slavery. No constitution can legitimize slavery, a preemptory norm from which no derogation is permitted. And this is not theory. In Puerto Rico today, prison regulation declares that leave is not a right nor a grace. Movements at total administrative discretion. Incarcerated people earn their freedom back through labor. These are the powers of ownership. That is slavery as the law defines it. Now understand what self-determination is being offered here. The people of Puerto Rico are told they may remove the slavery exception themselves, but they didn't put it there. They abolished slavery in 1873, and the U.S. put it back. Now that the burden of removing a jus cogens violation falls on the people, it was inflicted upon, to then have to ask the same government that imposed it for permission to remove it. We call this self-determination? A body that Puerto Rico does not fully elect gets to decide whether to honor a vote to end legalized slavery. This is not self-determination. That's asking for permission to end a crime against humanity, permission to abolish slavery. This committee would not approve that constitution today. It approved it in 1952.

Studies point to the generational trauma and the impact of colonization as contributing significantly to present-day health disparities, including high rates of chronic disease, cancer, obesity, mental illness, drug use, and other manifestations of trauma. Data show infant mortality rates of Native Hawaiian Pacific Islanders are 46% higher than national rates. Food insecurity, 41% higher than household nationally. 1 in 6, or 17%, live in poverty, greater than the national average and that of the state of Hawaiʻi at around 10%. However, while the North American state as a sovereign independent state commemorates two and a half centuries of freedom of democratic self-government, Puerto Rico continues to be the oldest colony in the world without having achieved its full independence and national sovereignty. At the same time, the support of the Democratic Party to statehood responds to— reflects a domestic political calculation which takes the form of rhetoric of rights and equality and is not a genuine effort at decolonization. Ladies and gentlemen, the political future of Puerto Rico must be decided in line with the universal principle of the free determination of peoples and their right to independence. Over the past 2 years, we have visited various offices of Republican congresspersons in Washington. Congressman Tom McClintock has spoken in favor of the independence of Puerto Rico. Which is the first public expression of support by Republican legislator since the creation of the Commonwealth in 1952. Likewise, I recently had a conversation with Republican Congressman John McGuire of Virginia, to whom I provided a draft legislation in favor of independence that Congressman McClinton will consider. Unfortunately, the current resident commissioner in Washington, Pablo José Hernández, has taken a step back in the process of decolonization by submitting a draft law similar to the failed H.R. 8393 Puerto Rican Status Act, but including the colonial territory as an option. This draft The law is unacceptable and does not have the support of the Republicans in Congress. Including the territory is equivalent to maintaining the door open to statehood and to perpetuate colonialism. For 128 years of United States colonialism and 533 years of colonial domination overall, after that, the time has finally comfort Puerto Rico to take its place among the free and sovereign nations of the world. Thank you very much. Long live free Puerto Rico.
I thank Mr. Rivera. I now recognize and invite Ms. Ana M. López to address the committee. Madam, you have the floor, please.

Thank you. My name is Ana María López López, and I'm speaking on behalf of Women United Against Genocide, a member of FDIM. We are a broad-based coalition of civic organizations. Women as givers of human life, transmitters of identity and culture, and as leaders within our communities. Make up more than 50% of Puerto Rico's population. The persistent colonial situation spanning 128 years has affected women and children more— most severely. Women were subjected to forced sterilization at a rate of 45% between 1940 and 1970, an act constituting genocide. Pervasive poverty affects women and children. Over 56% live below the poverty line. This poverty is disproportionate in compared to other U.S. jurisdictions. The rate is 3 times higher. Among families with 3 or more children, the poverty rate is 90%. Women are heads of household constituting 60% 60-67% of the population. This hunger, this constant lack of water in many municipalities and frequent power outages. Families face lack of affordable housing while land is handed over on a silver platter to foreign investors and billionaires who pay no taxes. Increasing levels of homelessness It is estimated that by the year 2050, Puerto Rico's population will shrink from 3 million to 2 million, driven by a steadily declining birth rate. More people are dying in Puerto Rico than they're being born. The forced migration and displacement of Puerto Ricans constitute genocide. I speak from personal experience. My family and village comprising of farmers and agriculture workers, have been victims of forced land expropriation twice: in 1930s by the U.S. military and in 2024, stripping us of a 200-year history and way of life. The colonial conditions present in Puerto Rico also manifest in our communities and neighborhoods within the United States. Puerto Ricans face constant racial discrimination, daily police violence, and displacement. Under the guise of democracy, our hostile colonial situation imposed by U.S. imperialism has denied us our inalienable right to sovereignty and independence in accordance with U.N. Resolution 1514/15. Let us be clear: achieving independence is the only decolonizing solution for Puerto Rico. For this reason, we live and we understand the devastation caused by genocide, military intervention, and—
I thank Ms. Ana López.
Thank you very much. ¡Viva Puerto Rico libre! ¡Viva!
I now invite Mr. Ricardo Quiles to address the committee. Sir, you have the floor, please.

Saludo. Greetings. My name is Ricardo Quiles. I'm a militant from Las Promesas, an organization that denounces the crime of colonialism and advocates for the independence of Puerto Rico. Today, as we've done for several years now, we come to you to denounce a crime against the people of Puerto Rico, a nation that has been subjected to military intervention by the United— governments of the United States since 1898, a nation that remains in a condition of colonial subjugation under an empire that, with the complicity of the local government, is displacing our people and destroying our natural resources. Our country is in a deplorable situation. Thousands are without water. Infrastructure is in decline. And our natural resources are being threatened by those who see Puerto Rico as a playground. Added to this, we have a fiscal oversight board imposed by the U.S. government, which 10 years on has continued to drive our country into misery and undermine our public university system. None of this would be possible without the complicity of a corrupt local government that maintains its power through lies, repression, fraud, and submission to the interests of those who seek to dispossess us of our land. Many people have come here today to denounce this criminal act. Some have done so while clinging to impossible dreams of colonial assimilation, bowing and scraping before the empire, begging for its attention. But the reality is that the only solution to our colonial condition is Freedom. It is our independence. It is the Constitution of the Republic of Puerto Rico. Millions of Puerto Ricans, both within and outside the archipelago, continue to ask: How much suffering? How much injustice? How much more evidence does the United Nations need to shoulder its responsibility and return Puerto Rico to the list of colonized territories? How much longer will it overlook the fact that the U.S. is violating its international obligations by keeping Puerto Rico under a colonial regime in disguise. There is little point coming year after year to repeat a truth that you already know and continue to ignore, just as you have ignored the Palestinian genocide. Your inaction and silence make you complicit in imperial violence. Today, we once again demand that the international community call Puerto Rico's reality what it is: a colony. We demand that the government of the United States be held accountable for the crime that it continues to commit against our people. The time has come to act. Puerto Rico deserves justice. Thank you very much. Long live a free Puerto Rico.
I thank Mr. Cueles. I now invite Ms. Lia Filo-Mata to address the committee. Madam, you have the floor. Good morning.

My name is Lía Fiolmata, and I represent the organization Power for Puerto Rico. We are here to ask this committee an urgent, long-overdue question: Why has the General Assembly never considered your resolutions on Puerto Rico? Since 1972, this committee has issued more than 40 resolutions to decolonize Puerto Rico, yet none have been moved to a vote in the General Assembly. Year after year, we come to this hearing to no avail. Must we remind you that we were excluded from the 1898 Treaty of Paris, where two imperial powers decided Puerto Rico's fate according to their own interests? Must we remind you of the many ways the United States consistently violates Section 748 of Article 73 because we are not a self-governing territory? The USA is deceiving in how it portrays its relationship with Puerto Rico. Domestically, we have little to no power over important aspects of our lives, such as trade and immigration policies, public benefits, government budget and spending with the imposition of an unelected fiscal control board, and many more. For the USA, Puerto Rico belongs to but is not part of this country. According to Supreme Court cases that continue to legitimize our unequal treatment. Yet before the UN and the world, the USA argues that Puerto Rico's constitution is proof that we are self-governing and not a colony. The United States lies about our relationship, and its blatant misrepresentation must end. The USA's treatment of Puerto Rico has always been one —of imposition, domination, and control. Stemming from a military invasion, we have always been subjugated to the empire, used and abused, for example, to fight in U.S. wars, as guinea pigs in medical experimentation, and as a military outpost for U.S. war actions. This treatment is contrary to the principles of sovereignty and democracy upon which the UN was founded. As the oldest colony in the world, Puerto Rico is tired of being ignored. After waiting over 50 years for our matter to be heard in the General Assembly, it is time for you to act. We yearn for our country to be free from colonial rule, not by annexation to the empire that strangles us, but by charting our own path in the world. You must demand that our right to sovereignty be voted on in the General Assembly once and for all.
I thank Ms. Mata. I now invite Mr. Rafael Oliveira Citron to address the committee. Sir, you have the floor, please. Microphone, please, for the petitioner. Thank you. Please proceed.
Hello. Thank you. Can I reset the timer?
Uh, can we start the timer over, please? Thank you.
All right.

No se puede. You can't wake up before you dream. Just for a moment, dream of a free Puerto Rico that is truly yours. One where the sun warms you, lights your home without electricity shortages preventing you from reading. One where Tommy can graduate and doesn't have to move away, where his smile and ambition to thrive are not lost. One where there is no lack of water where beaches belong to the people. One where our crops sway in the fields and abundance fills your dining room. One where an egg doesn't cost the price of a house and where people can both buy food and refrigerate it. One where we live happily and healthily in a land shared with our families and our culture, where we can hear the music of our prosperity carried on the air. It's our dream to wake up and see the sun. Let us Let's not allow them to take away our duty and our opportunity to live. Land and housing. What you're imagining isn't the American dream. This is the Puerto Rican dream. It is yours. It is ours. And it belongs to no one else. A Puerto Rican identity that represents us in all of our aspirations in life, governance, the economy, health, food, everything, developing our ability to solve problems and in the process building our own Foundation of support. My name is Rafael Oribe La Cintrón. Thank you, committee, for the opportunity to speak.

Even though you supposedly united to end colonialism by organizing this committee 54 years ago, us Puerto Ricans have been the ones needing to come together to solve our colonial crisis because your empty words, 43 resolutions in without action, have led us to ruin. While the news reflects how this institution bends regularly to the pressures of powers around them, we don't. Porque somos boricuas. Our strength is not our unity of strategy, rather our strategy of unity. And while we take time from our jobs to come here and say the same things every year, it feels like you are too scared to do your job and fully execute on the task of decolonizing the Earth's oldest colony. Yes, we understand that Puerto Rico has a right to self-determine, that we have been abandoned, neglected, sanctioned, displaced, priced out, and legally enslaved. Yes, we understand that Wall Street and fiscal control boards should not govern our public services. We understand that developers with international banks should not buy our protected nature reserves from mega-billion-dollar tax havens like Ascensia. We understand that our local government should not then go pass laws that limit our speech to allow them to buy that land, like PC-25 and 310. We understand that our cost of living should not be tied to our inability to trade with other countries. And we understand that you should not be allowing our most corrupt politicians to come and speak on behalf of the Puerto Rican people. ¿Qué vas a hacer? What else are you going to do about it? How are you going to hold the U.S. accountable? How are you going to help us fulfill the Puerto Rican dream?

Por eso le hablo a ustedes. That's why today I primarily speak to my own people here, because this chamber is not going to resolve our problems for us. We must take responsibility for our own destiny, build our own path, and walk it at the same time. May this message reach all of those who eat mofongo, tostones, and roast pork, who want to bury the pitorro in the ground without having to hide from the realities of living as a colony.
I thank Mr. Rafael Citron. I now invite Miss Claire Belle Avila to address the committee. Madam, you have the floor, please.

Two months ago, House Bill PC-310 was signed into law. This law denies the people their legal rights by allowing further development on the island. This represents more environmental disasters, economic discrimination, increased displacement, and a declaration that the opinion of the people is worth nothing. We don't believe that the reason the island of Puerto Rico is facing a level of poverty is a direct result of the policies imposed by the United States. If a law of this magnitude were to be proposed here, it would be framed as an affront to human rights. However, the corrupt government of Puerto Rico was able to pass it without the will of the people. But my story shows me that people didn't— my people did not give up. For more than 500 years, we've resisted cultural death, and in the last 2 years, we've resisted Proyecto Esencia through a struggle for life for both our citizens and our environmental environment. My name is Claribel Avila. I'm the daughter of two colonial migrants from Ladis. As a part of the diaspora, I understand that the disconnection I feel from my ancestral land where my grandparents are buried was intentionally designed by an empire that fears the power of our culture. The time has come to reconnect with that unbreakable culture Above all, it's time to dream. It's not enough to loudly reject the empire. We must reconnect with the Puerto Rican dream, a dream that is absurd in its vastness, as ambitious as the Puerto Rican people themselves, a future so rich, so inspiring that it becomes irresistible to join in building toward that future. It is necessary to exercise our creativity and begin to see the world not as the colonizers have painted it, painted it, impossible to change, but rather what it can be. So I ask you, what is the Puerto Rico of your dreams? How do you see it through your senses? For me, Puerto Rico is the Caribbean sun caressing my skin. It is the smell of alcapurrias freshly fried by my grandmother. It can be heard through the sound of dominoes when capicú is played, and in the laughter when we play together as a family. After decades of bearing witness to our struggle before this committee, one thing is very clear to me: only the people can save the people. The diaspora plays an important role. No matter who you are, Puerto Rico is yours, and Puerto Rico needs you and needs us to dream. Long live free Puerto Rico.
I thank Miss Claribel Avila. I now invite Mr. Michael Vera to address the committee. Sir, you have the floor, please.

Thank you, Madam Chair.

Colonialism is not merely a historical condition, it is a present situation that corrupts the decisions that affect the colonized. We reject their crock of lies. They want everything privatized and we're getting ostracized. These highest bidders are critters laughing all the way to Bank. Have you heard of the latest escándalo involving Politanc, founded by this guy named Frank, Francisco Dominic, who was hired by Governor Jago, scheming for the rich. She's the head of the class while he's— she's the head of the class in the school of epic fail. He's her chief of staff making rules. Follow the trail. Another year we see a monopoly, no democracy. I want my people to be free with sovereignty and integrity. All across Puerto Rico, the people been organizing. The government's antagonizing with propaganda advertising, calling us los pelúes that are causing revolú. But I got some news, no nos vamos.

They're not going to leave us. They won't leave us behind. I blue.

Their desperation is obvious. They're imploding from within. All the statehood lobbyists are from the same engine. PNP, PPD, vote for PC3D. So now the Senate floor is doing more to ensure violations of our coast to the shore, for they'll ignore a community that can't afford the price to retort and report a case in the court. In short, they have cemented their demented incentives to favor the rich in our port. We demand accountability. They have no credibility. En el tesillo, they give out permits for the construction that leads to the destruction of our land and the erasure of our gente en Puerto Rico. Wannabe Anglo-Saxons are forcing the displacement. They're blatant with their actions, endorsing manipulation. They're constantly engañando and shamelessly bambeteando. Using religion to further division, but the people are despertando. They're allowed to run amok as long as they keep us stuck under the thumb. They suck because they don't give a truck filled with water due to the ruptured aqueduct. Neglected structures collapsing while USA hosts the World Cup. They play dumb while keeping the pueblo dependent on crumbs. While the foreigners come, they drinking our rum and they stealing our land and our funds. They want us on our knees to bow down and salute to the operation boot in a suit that continues to loot. From New York to El Morro, no ha proyecto esencia. Ojo en Cabo Rojo, esto es nuestra herencia. El padre de la patria me dijo, no te canses.

The father of our homeland said, don't tire.

Tito Rafael wrote the song Preciosa before Benito had us yelling, acho, pero eres otra cosa. The duty of Puerto Ricans is to defend and protect. We can't claim to be Boricua and accept the disrespect.. It's that feeling that we get. It's that pride that we project. We might sing off-key, but it's those lyrics. It's what those lyrics, those lyrics represent.

Preciosa te llaman los hijos de la libertad.

¡Que viva Puerto Rico libre!
I thank, I thank Mr. Vera. I thank the petitioner. I now invite Mr. Maximo Riviera Lopez to address the committee. Sir, you have the floor, please.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair, distinguished members of the Special Committee on Decolonization of the United Nations. My name is Maximino Rivera López, and I come before you on behalf of our nation and in my capacity as President of the Committee on the Diaspora of The Puerto Rican Independence Party. For more than 125 years, Puerto Rico has been subjected to colonial domination by the United States, suffering a political status which is in all regards intolerable and is incompatible with the most basic principles of democracy and human rights. The US Congress Commonwealth continues to exercise plenary powers over our nation, dictating our laws, controlling our international trade, and block— blocking our full development. The myth of the so-called self-government of the Commonwealth has been fully revealed through the decisions of the U.S. Supreme Court in the Sanchez Valle case and through the imposition of the PROMESA Act by the Congress. Through this harmful law, the United States imposed a fiscal control board that is dictatorial, which is not elected by the Puerto Rican people, which operates as a collecting agency for Wall Street Wall Street at the cost— while imposing devastating austerity measures. Under this colonial yoke, the average family income in Puerto Rico has stalled at just $25,000 per year, just one-third of the U.S. average. This profound economic and social crisis has led to a massive exodus forcing hundreds of thousands of our compatriots to leave their land in quest for their survival, joining the queues of the diaspora that I join here— ranks of the diaspora that I represent here. We recognize that since 1992, this special committee has issued annual resolutions reaffirming, constantly reaffirming, the inalienable right of the people of Puerto Rico to self-determination and independence. Nonetheless, the persistence of this indignant colonial paradox means that we need to take one step further. It's not enough to make statements. It is essential for the international community step up the diplomatic pressure on the United States. Our country cannot continue to be treated as a territory where the consent of governors is null and void and whether citizens are used as a disguise for the subordination. Maintaining a colony in the Caribbean in the midst of the 21st century is a moral stain on any nation that self-proclaims itself.

I thank Mr. Lopez. I thank Mr. Lopez. I now— thank you, sir. Thank you. I now— thank you. I now recognize and invite Ms. Sonia Santiago Hernandez to address the committee. Madam, you have the floor, please. Thank you.

Distinguished members of the Special Committee on Decolonization, please receive the warm greetings from Madres Against War, Mothers Against War, which is a pacifist organization founded in Puerto Rico in 2003 by mothers of Puerto Rican soldiers. We denounce that colonialism suffered by Puerto Rico is not only seen through the lack of —of political and economic sovereignty, but also a profound and persistent militarization of our territory and our society. For 128 years of U.S. domination, Puerto Rico has been used as a strategic enclave for military operations in the Caribbean and Latin America. Our archipelago has served to establish military bases, training camps, belligerent maneuvers and geopolitical operations for the United States that has served interests outside the will of our people. Military installations have been built affecting communities, limiting the use of land, and conditioning the socioeconomic and cultural development of our nation. We denounce the military presence of the U.S. and the use of Puerto Rico as a platform for regional operations, such as the invasion of Venezuela on the 3rd of January. Thousands of Puerto Ricans are currently in military— in the military service. They find an alternative there. This decision is being conditioned by poverty and inequality more than by true will. More than 200,000 Puerto Ricans have been— have fought wars on behalf of the U.S. Many have come home physically and emotionally sick. We demand the promotion of environmental cleaning for areas affected by military activities to address the health of those affected and also the veterans, and for us to reject any use of Puerto Rico as a platform for military operations or interventions in kindred countries in the Caribbean, such as Cuba, Latin America, or any other region in the world. Maternity is love and military is death. The end of military bases in Puerto Rico. Long live Puerto Rico.
I thank Miss Hernandez. I thank Miss Hernandez. I now invite Miss Annette Falcon to address the committee. Madam, you have the floor, please.

Thank you very much.

Bueno día. Good afternoon. My name is Annette Falcon. This is the third year that I come to the UN committee. The first time that I spoke here, many saw that I— we could have a fourth option, because being a U.S. citizen without dignified representation in Washington and with a law that is affecting us has devastated us. All Puerto Ricans know that we do not want to continue being a colony of anyone. In the 128 years, Puerto Rico has not become a state, and it will not be one. The current status of the Commonwealth isn't a state, it is an associated state, because what the United States is— what they say is what they have done. Independence without a robust plan to overcome failure will not happen. What we need is to consolidate the political party that we want to build to ensure that we could be the 18th autonomous community of Spain. Puerto Ricans know that we have always had a cultural reality that we share with Spain, that that's never gone away until we had our own government, and it will not until we have our own government with them. Um, we still continue to see, uh, Spanish influences on— in our culture, in them, in the mass, and on our dining tables. We continue to see the cries of our heart. Let us remember— let Spain remember Puerto Rico. This isn't a romanticism of the past, as some claim. Spain is our day-to-day— from— it is a It's a story that remains living in Puerto Rico. When we talk about reunification with Spain, we're not talking about conquering it or going backwards. The question shouldn't be whether Puerto Rico can become Spanish again. The true question is whether we are ready to recognize that many aspects— in many aspects, we've never stopped being Spanish. For this reason, I respectfully say to the government of Spain and to His Majesty King Felipe VI to restore Spanish nationality to Puerto Ricans who are requesting it. We want to go home. 128 years.

An official plebiscite is in order. Let's make Puerto Rico Spain again. Ole!
Well, it's better than being a colonist.
I thank Ms. Falcon. I now invite Mr. José Proventud. Mr. José Proventud to address the committee. Sir, you have the floor.

Members of the committee, my name is Jové Póventud. I'm from Guayama, Puerto Rico. Puerto Rico overwhelmingly decided in March of 1898 that it wanted to be independent or did not want to be Anglo-Saxon. During the war with the United States, one of the key negotiators of the Treaty of Paris, 1898, was Whitelaw Reid, editor, director, and owner of the New York Tribune. He said, and I quote, "These islands—Puerto Rico, Cuba, Guam, and the Philippines—should be permanently governed as colonies, always excluding the most remote idea of allowing them, admitting them, to the federal union." Article 9 of the Paris Treaty deprived unilaterally Puerto Ricans of their Spanish citizenship. Citizenship without consulting the population of the island. Documents of the negotiations conserved in the Library of Congress show that Spain, Spain gave up under intense military and diplomatic pressure. The regent queen opposed tenaciously but did not obtain any results. After having been Puerto Rico autonomous territory and part and parcel of the Spanish kingdom, the United States degraded it into a colony, an extraction colony, as Mr. Reed requested. In 1900 began scholar doctrina— school doctrination hidden under a project of literacy with the purpose of promoting a separate identity from our Spanish tradition. We were separated from Spain without being consulted. Today, 128 years later, we request that you permit us to consider all alternatives of decolonization, including the reintegration with Spain. Today I come here as a representative of a legitimate and necessary alternative because it is a force that is constantly growing that under any— under no pretext can be negated as a right to— as a decolonizing option. We respect other options, but we don't agree with them. We've been denied statehood for for 120 years for reasons that continue to be for insular states. To deny the reintegration with Spain to prevent Puerto Ricans fully exercise— is to prevent Puerto Ricans from fully exercising their inalienable right to self-determination. We request this committee that delegates from the Kingdom of Spain, United States, and Puerto Rico meet and reach an agreement tripartite agreement that the Spanish Parliament extends Spanish nationality as an option to all Puerto Ricans with ancestors that were born before 1898, that the reunification of Spain be included in a future referendum of self-determination. There will be full— there won't be self-determination without reintegration. As politically, if we're Spanish politically, we'll be Spanish in spirit. Long live Puerto Rico, long live Spain. Spain, and long live the King. Thank you.
I thank Mr. Proventud. I now invite Mr. Hadoro Sare to address the committee. Sir, you have the floor, please. Mr. Sare.

Yes, honorable chair, distinguished member of the special committee. Excellencies and respected delegates, thank you for the opportunity to address the United Nations Committee on Decolonization during this important meeting concerning Puerto Rico. My name is Harold Rosario. I appear before you as the United States' extended congressional delegate for Puerto Rico and also as the founder and CEO of SpaceSys, an aerospace and defense company with entity and partnership across Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Europe, Asia, and the United States of America. I speak today with deep respect for the people of Puerto Rico, for the principles of the United Nations, and for the longstanding commitment of this committee to the dignity, equality, and self-determination of all people. Puerto Rico's political status has remained unresolved for far too long. For generations, the people of Puerto Rico have lived under a political arrangement that affects their democratic representation, economic development, disaster recovery, public health, education, infrastructure, and long-term future. These are not abstract issues. They affect families, communities, students, workers, and future generations. The central issue before us is simple but profound: the people of Puerto Rico deserve a clear, fair, democratic, and internationally respected path to determine and implement their political future. Any meaningful solution must be rooted in the will of the Puerto Rican people, expressed through a transparent and legitimate process, and followed by concrete action. The people of Puerto Rico have voted multiple times in favor of statehood. Their will has been expressed through democratic participation, and that will deserve to be respected. In my view, statehood is the best path forward because it offers full equality, full democratic representation, and a permanent place for Puerto Rico within the American constitutional family. For this reason, the question of Puerto Rico should not remain a repeated annual discussion without meaningful progress. The voices of the Puerto Rican people deserve not only to be heard, but to be respected and acted upon. I therefore respectfully urge this committee to work with the United States and international partners in good faith to help ensure that the democratically expressed will of the Puerto Rican people become a reality. I ask this committee to support meaningful action towards statehood and to call for a fair, transparent, and binding process through which Puerto Rico's chosen future will be respected and implemented. This matter is not only about political status. It is about fairness. It is about human dignity. It's about the right of a people to participate fully in shaping their own future. Self-determination should not be a slogan. Equality should not be postponed. Democracy should not be incomplete. I hope that today's discussion will contribute to real progress, not only through words, but through meaningful steps forwards. Puerto Rico deserves clarity. Puerto Rico deserves equality. Puerto Rico deserves action. Thank you for your attention.
I thank Mr. Serré. I now recognize and invite Mr. Manuel Francisco O'Neill to address the committee. Mr. O'Neill, you have the floor, please.

I speak on behalf of the Vermont-Puerto Rico Solidarity Committee. The abolitionist Frederick Douglass, when expressing his sentiments on the meaning of the Declaration of Independence to Black Americans, acknowledged that while the document recognized that all men were were born free and equal and possessed certain inalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. The truth in practice was that many persons remained enslaved. He conceded that the authors of the Declaration of Independence were learned men worthy of recognition, but they were not perfect or without sin, and that the aspirations expressed within the Declaration's text needed to be extended to all persons. The U.S. Declaration of Independence, influenced by the governance practices of the Hondasani Confederacy and authored by an elite class of colonial settlers, later turned independentistas, rejected colonialism, and later created a constitutional rule-based governance system with three co-equal branches of government, a Bill of Rights, and the guarantee of due process and equal protection to all persons, and codified the principles that government and its agents derive their powers from the governed, the people. Puerto Ricans understand the sentiments expressed in the Declaration, as we are not strangers to the dynamics of colonialism, a system that for the sake of profit has exploited labor, expropriates natural resources, subjugates peoples and cultures, impoverishes the majority of people, criminalizes resistance, imprisons the resister, and steals from the perpetrator and the victim their humanity. And neither are we unpracticed in the struggle to rid ourselves of an external power that prevents us from organizing ourselves for the purpose of self-government. For more than 530 years, we have struggled through various means to establish a governance system democratically organized and beholding exclusively to the will of the Puerto Rican people. Like Frederick Douglass, we too are conflicted. Acquired by the United States without our consent, we remain in possession of but not an integrated part of the United States. U.S. citizenship was imposed upon us, but we have no representation in the U.S. Senate or meaningful representation in the U-House, in the United States House of Representatives, and we are not eligible to vote for U.S. president. In 1952, the Estado Libre Asociado granted Puerto Rico autonomy with regards to internal matters, but its constitution, laws, and jurisprudence had to conform with those of the United States. We have participated in, to no meaningful end, status plebiscites which run contrary to the truth enumerated in both the U.S. and U.N. declarations. Requires us to again suffer the indignity of having to vote as to whether we want to be free, and which only obfuscates, delays, and thwarts an otherwise simple process by which colonized people or enslaved persons free themselves from colonialism and bondage. And for more than—
I thank Mr. O'Neill. I now— I thank Mr. O'Neill. I now invite Mr. Walter Alomar to address the committee. Mr. Alomar, you have the floor, please. Thank you.

My name is Walter Gualterio Alomar. I appear before this committee to address a common argument against Puerto Rico's independence, that Puerto Rico could not survive economically as a sovereign nation. The facts tell a different story. According to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Puerto Rico's gross domestic product exceeds $113 billion annually. That is a larger economy than dozens of independent nations including Jamaica, Iceland, and the Bahamas. Puerto Rico is not a poor nation. Puerto Rico is a nation whose economic potential is constrained by a colonial relationship. Puerto Rico currently imports 85% of its food. According to the agricultural experts and the— Puerto Rico Department of Agriculture, the island has the capacity to significantly increase local food production. Reducing food imports by just 20% would keep $1.3 billion circulating within the local economy instead of sending that money overseas. Puerto Rico is a global manufacturing center. The pharmaceutical and medical device industry can generate $50 billion in economic activity annually. Puerto Rico manufactures many of the medicines consumed throughout the United States and remains is one of the world's leading pharmaceutical production hubs. Yet Puerto Rico cannot negotiate its own trade agreements with Europe, Latin America, Africa, or Asia. Every independent nation that has that right, Puerto Rico does not. Tourism provides another example. Puerto Rico receives approximately 4 to 5 million visitors annually.
